questions.q: Define deindustrialisation in the context of colonial India and state the two-fold motive of the British government behind it.
questions.a: Deindustrialisation is the systematic decline of indigenous handicraft industries without replacement by a modern industrial base. The two-fold British motive: (1) reduce India to a raw material supplier for British industries, and (2) turn India into a captive market for British manufactured goods. A wrong answer that only mentions "decline of handicrafts" without the two-fold motive reveals the student misses the intentional policy design — they see outcome but not colonial agency.

questions.q: Explain why the famous Daccai muslin industry collapsed even though its products were globally renowned for quality, using the concepts of discriminatory tariffs and railway integration.
questions.a: Daccai muslin collapsed because British machine-made cloth entered India duty-free (or at nominal tariffs) while Indian textiles faced 70-80% duties in Britain. Railways accelerated this by cheaply transporting British cloth to interior villages and raw cotton to ports, undercutting local weavers' cost structure. A wrong answer blaming "lack of demand" or "inferior quality" reveals the student ignores the asymmetric trade policy — they apply free-market logic to a rigged colonial market.

questions.q: In 1850, India exported £3 million worth of raw cotton to Britain and imported £8 million worth of British cotton textiles. By 1900, raw cotton exports rose to £25 million but textile imports surged to £40 million. Calculate the change in India's textile trade balance and explain what this reveals about the nature of deindustrialisation.
questions.a: 1850 trade balance: -£5 million (imports > exports). 1900 trade balance: -£15 million. The deficit tripled despite raw cotton exports growing 8-fold. This reveals deindustrialisation was not merely decline — it was active replacement: India became a raw material appendage while its domestic market was captured by British manufactures. A student calculating only percentage changes without interpreting the structural shift misses the core economic transformation.

questions.q: Compare the regional concentration of cotton textile mills (Maharashtra/Gujarat) and jute mills (Bengal) at independence. Analyse how this lopsided pattern reflected colonial economic interests rather than India's resource endowments.
questions.a: Cotton mills clustered in western India (Indian capital, near cotton-growing tracts and Bombay port for export). Jute mills concentrated in Bengal (British capital, near jute-growing areas and Calcutta port for export to global markets). Both served export-oriented colonial needs — not domestic industrial diversification. A wrong answer citing "natural resource availability" alone ignores that capital ownership, port access, and export orientation drove location — not balanced regional development.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The establishment of Tata Iron and Steel Company (1907) and a few cotton/jute mills proves British rule laid the foundations of modern Indian industry."
questions.a: The statement is misleading. TISCO and textile mills were isolated enclaves — less than 2% of GDP, no capital goods industry (machine tools), no backward/forward linkages, and public sector confined to railways/ports serving colonial extraction. True industrialisation requires a self-sustaining ecosystem of capital goods, which was deliberately prevented. A student agreeing with the statement confuses "presence of factories" with "industrialisation" — they miss the structural incompleteness.

questions.q: Construct a causal chain diagram (minimum 6 links) showing how British land revenue policy → commercialisation of agriculture → decline of handicrafts → rural unemployment → increased pressure on land → stagnant agricultural wages. Use specific policy instruments (zamindari, railways, tariffs) at each step.
questions.a: Zamindari system (fixed revenue dates) → forced cash-crop cultivation (indigo, cotton) → raw cotton exported via railways → British machine-cloth imported duty-free → village weavers lose livelihood → displaced artisans become landless labourers → labour supply surges → agricultural wages stagnate. A poor answer lists factors without causal arrows — they treat events as parallel rather than sequential, missing the cumulative causation central to colonial political economy.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ refers to the deliberate and systematic decline of India's indigenous handicraft and artisan industries under British colonial rule, driven by a two-fold policy: transforming India into a supplier of raw materials (cotton, jute, indigo) for British factories and a captive market for British machine-made manufactured goods, without allowing a corresponding modern industrial base to emerge.

Fill in the blank: Imagine a ______ in 1830s Dhaka producing legendary Daccai muslin — once worn by Mughal emperors and European royalty — now unable to sell a single bolt because Lancashire mill-cloth floods the local bazaar at one-tenth the price.
What is Deindustrialisation? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Deindustrialisation refers to the deliberate and systematic decline of India's indigenous handicraft and artisan industries under British colonial rule, driven by a two-fold policy: transforming India into a supplier of raw materials (cotton, jute, indigo) for British factories and a captive market for British machine-made manufactured.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Deindustrialisation?
questions.a: Students believe deindustrialisation happened because Indian handicrafts were "inefficient" or "could not compete" with modern technology.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the two-fold motive behind British deindustrialisation, trace the causal chain from discriminatory tariffs to artisan unemployment, and evaluate why modern industry failed to absorb displaced handicraft workers using data on industrial composition and regional concentration.
